summary: An April 1st humorous RFC offering guidelines for identification and security at IETF meetings, with special attention paid to a sub-group it calls "facial hairius extremis". It is a joke.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke imagines facial hair causing mistaken identity at IETF meetings. It offers lighthearted advice to check before assuming who someone is.

questions: why does rfc 2323 discuss facial hair
subtitle: An April 1st joke about mistaken identity at IETF meetings.

tldr.problem: The memo jokes that people with similar facial hair may be mistaken for one another at IETF meetings.
tldr.mechanism: It advises people seeking someone to confirm identity and those being sought to signal whether they are the person.
tldr.outcome: This April 1st document is entertainment, not a real security or identification standard.

facts.label: Claimed long-term facial hair at IETF

today: RFC 2323 is an Informational April 1st joke document about identification at IETF conferences.

sections.title: The Mistaken-Identity Premise
sections.content:
The memo says it is intended as entertainment and does not specify an Internet standard. Its subject is a group it labels “facial hairius extremis,” and it jokingly presents facial hair as a cause of confusion at IETF conferences.

It recounts anecdotes about people being mistaken for researchers with similar descriptions. These are presented as the motivation for the memo's mock guidelines.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke is that many conference attendees have beards, so descriptions may fit several people. The RFC turns that social confusion into mock security guidance.

sections.title: Anecdotes and Claimed Evidence
sections.content:
The author contrasts an estimate of less than 20% of men with long-term facial hair in personal experience with a claim of up to 60% among men at IETF meetings. The memo distinguishes long-term facial hair from temporary goatees.

It uses these figures and stories of mistaken identity as comic evidence. They are claims made by the humorous document, not rules for identifying people.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC uses humorous estimates and anecdotes to support its premise. Its point is that a beard alone does not identify a person.

sections.title: The Proposed Social Guidelines
sections.content:
People looking for someone are told to check that they have the correct person before starting a conversation. Those with facial hair are advised to correct a mistaken name politely or use a wave and a head movement to signal yes or no.

The memo frames the advice as a shared responsibility: seekers should ask, and the person being sought can respond clearly. The RFC closes with a lighthearted hope that the guidance helps.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask someone if you have the right person before assuming. If someone calls you by the wrong name, politely correct them.
